docs.title: Compatibility at a glance
docs.text:
• Physical SDK firmware requirement: 2.0.4 or newer.
  • Supported hosts: Linux x86_64, Linux ARM64, and Windows x86_64.
  • Supported Python versions: 3.10–3.13.
  • macOS is not currently supported.
  • The Pulsar App controls one physical actuator at a time.

Need help? Visit Support or FAQ and Support.

docs.title: Support
docs.text:
For product and integration support, contact PULSAR HRI:

  • Email: support.dt@pulsarhri.com
  • Monday–Thursday: 08:00–17:00 GMT
  • Friday: 08:00–13:00 GMT

Include the actuator model, firmware version, host operating system, connection type, and a concise description of what happened.

For Developer Hub bugs or documentation requests, open an issue:

github.com/PulsarHRI/pulsarhri.github.io/issues

Do not post credentials, private packages, serial numbers, or other sensitive information in a public issue.

docs.title: Which interface should I use first?
docs.text: Use Pulsar App for one physical actuator without code, direct USB with Pulsar Python SDK for Python development, CAN FD for several physical actuators, and VirtualWorld when no hardware is available and you want to explore the actuator's performance to your specific project.

docs.title: Which firmware is required by Pulsar SDK?
docs.text: Physical actuators require firmware 2.0.4 or newer. Update Firmware if an update is needed.

docs.title: Is macOS supported?
docs.text: No. Current supported hosts are Linux x86_64, Linux ARM64, and Windows x86_64.

docs.title: Does Pulsar App control virtual actuators?
docs.text: No. Pulsar App currently controls one physical actuator at a time through USB. Use Pulsar SDK for other phsycal/virtual actuators needs.

docs.title: Do you support EtherCAT?
docs.text: EtherCAT support is planned for Q1 2027 through native board integration, or through an EtherCAT-to-CAN adapter if you own CAN-based Pulsar Actuator.

docs.title: Where are the Rust SDK docs?
docs.text: The Pulsar Rust SDK is coming soon. Its section will be expanded when the crate, examples, and reference are released.

docs.title: Open Pulsar Python SDK issues
docs.text:
The following issues are currently tracked for Pulsar Python SDK and will be fixed in a future release:

  • #1 — Reconnect isolation: queued transport-loss handling affects a newly reconnected actuator session.
  • #2 — Physical-domain validation: PulsarActuatorReal doesn't reject VirtualWorld as a domain.
  • #3 — Stale telemetry recovery: enable() is allowed to recover the actuators to operational state without clearing the faults first.
  • #4 — Co-simulation ergonomics: a future bulk exchange helper should return elapsed ticks and telemetry while retaining the low-level step() API.

For help with a current application, use Support or open an issue in the Developer Hub repository.

docs.title: AUGUR Digital Twin
docs.text: AUGUR Digital Twin provides validated virtual models of PULSE actuators for software development, controller testing, and robot co-simulation. The same control algorithms run at 20 kHz in the digital twin and in the physical actuator firmware. The software interfaces are designed to let PULSAR HRI Virtual and Real actuators be controlled using the same function calls.

docs.text:
The remaining differences reflect how virtual and physical actuators operate:

  • Initialization and communication: Initialize a virtual actuator in software; connect a real actuator and communicate with it over its data bus.
  • External load: A real actuator experiences the load applied to its shaft. In a virtual simulation, pass the load explicitly (for example, from a physics engine) or choose a load for the simulation.

docs.title: Co-simulation coupling
docs.text: AUGUR Digital Twin

docs.title: Co-simulation coupling
docs.text:
AUGUR can be coupled to any multibody simulator that can evaluate the joint load produced by a robot model at an imposed joint state.

The coupling has one essential ownership rule:

  • AUGUR owns and integrates each coupled actuator's position and velocity.
  • The external simulator owns the robot links, inertia, gravity, contacts, constraints, and other mechanism dynamics.

Do not let both systems integrate the same joint. The simulator must calculate the load for an AUGUR-owned joint without forward-integrating that joint or applying a second actuator model to it.

docs.title: AUGUR's Interface
docs.text:
For co-simulation, each virtual actuator can be treated as a stateful function:

\[ \left(x_{a,k+1}, q_{k+1}, \dot q_{k+1}\right) = F_{\mathrm{AUGUR}}\left(u_k, \tau_{L,k}, \Delta t_c\right), \]

where:

  • \(x_a\) is AUGUR's internal actuator state which includes all values reported by the real/physical actuator;
  • \(u\) is the command sent through Pulsar SDK;
  • \(\tau_L\) is the load at the actuator output shaft, in N·m;
  • \(q\) and \(\dot q\) are output-shaft position and velocity, in rad and rad/s;
  • \(\Delta t_c\) is the coupling interval.

AUGUR contains its own dynamics and integrator. The external simulator therefore receives \(q\) and \(\dot q\) from AUGUR and returns the load \(\tau_L\) required by the robot mechanism.

Use the same positive direction for the AUGUR output shaft and the corresponding robot joint. Pass the simulator's required joint load to AUGUR in that natural joint sign; no additional sign inversion is needed.

docs.title: Robot dynamics
docs.text:
For \(n\) coupled joints, a robot model can be written as

\[ M(q)\ddot q + h(q, \dot q) = \tau_L + \tau_{\mathrm{ext}}, \]

where:

  • \(M(q)\) is the joint-space mass matrix;
  • \(h(q, \dot q)\) contains gravity, Coriolis, centrifugal, passive, constraint, and contact effects represented by the simulator;
  • \(\tau_{\mathrm{ext}}\) contains any separately applied generalized forces that might be in the simulation, like contacts, interaction forces, etc.;
  • \(\tau_L\) is the generalized effort that the coupled actuators must provide.

The external simulator evaluates the corresponding inverse-dynamics problem:

\[ \tau_L = M(q)\ddot q + h(q, \dot q) - \tau_{\mathrm{ext}}. \]

In practice, use the simulator's inverse-dynamics or generalized-effort result rather than assembling these terms manually. Contacts and constraints may require the simulator's own solver.

Do not duplicate/define motor rotor inertia, reflected gearbox inertia, drivetrain friction, motor/actuator damping, or joint limits, these are either already represented by AUGUR or can be set as parameters, like limits for example. On the other hand, keep link inertia, gravity, mechanism damping or springs, contacts, constraints, and externally applied forces in the robot model. Basically anything that is inside the actuator's envlope is modeled by AUGUR, anything attached to it, should be defined in the simulator.

docs.title: Coupling timestep
docs.text:
AUGUR's internal timestep is

\[ \Delta t_a = 50\ \mu\mathrm{s} = \frac{1}{20{,}000}\ \mathrm{s}. \]

Choose a coupling interval that is an integer multiple of this timestep:

\[ \Delta t_c = N\Delta t_a, \qquad N \in \mathbb{N}^{+}. \]

For example, a 1000 Hz exchange rate has \(\Delta t_c=0.001\) s and \(N=20\) AUGUR ticks. Smaller coupling intervals reduce the one-exchange load delay and usually improve stability. All actuators in one VirtualWorld must advance together.

docs.title: Exchange algorithm
docs.text:
This is an explicit co-simulation scheme. During exchange \(k\), AUGUR uses the load calculated at the previous exchange.

  1. Hold \(\tau_{L,k-1}\) constant and advance every virtual actuator by \(\Delta t_c\).
  2. Read the new output-shaft state \(q_k\) and \(\dot q_k\) from AUGUR.
  3. If needed, you can also estimate acceleration from the exchange-rate velocity difference which could improve the simulator's stability. The currently validated estimator applies a first-order 10 Hz low-pass filter:

$$ \ddot q_k^{\mathrm{raw}} = \frac{\dot q_k-\dot q_{k-1}}{\Delta t_c}, $$

$$ \alpha = 1-e^{-2\pi(10)\Delta t_c}, $$

$$ \ddot q_k = \ddot q_{k-1} + \alpha\left(\ddot q_k^{\mathrm{raw}}-\ddot q_{k-1}\right). $$

  1. Initialize \(\dot q_{-1}\) and \(\ddot q_{-1}\) to zero. The filter limits load noise caused by differentiating quantized velocity, especially near contacts and constraints. Changing the filter changes the coupled dynamics and requires new convergence and energy validation.
  2. Impose \(q_k\), \(\dot q_k\), and \(\ddot q_k\) on the corresponding robot joints without advancing those joint coordinates in the external simulator.
  3. Refresh the simulator's kinematics, contacts, and constraints, then evaluate inverse dynamics or the equivalent generalized-effort calculation.
  4. Read the required joint load \(\tau_{L,k}\), accounting once for any separately applied generalized forces already included in the simulator result.
  5. Pass \(\tau_{L,k}\) directly to AUGUR for the next exchange.

In compact form:

\[ \tau_{L,k-1} \xrightarrow{\ F_{\mathrm{AUGUR}}\ } (q_k,\dot q_k) \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{differentiate/filter\ if\ needed}\ } \ddot q_k \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{robot\ inverse\ dynamics}\ } \tau_{L,k}. \]

docs.title: External simulator requirements
docs.text:
The simulator or its integration layer written by you must be able to:

  • represent the robot's multibody dynamics, contacts, and constraints;
  • accept imposed \(q\), \(\dot q\), and optional \(\ddot q\) for AUGUR-owned joints;
  • update kinematics and constraints without forward-integrating those joints;
  • calculate the generalized joint effort required by the imposed motion;
  • expose that effort in N·m for each coupled revolute joint.

Loading URDF, MJCF, SDF, or OpenUSD does not by itself guarantee these capabilities. A simulator that can only forward-integrate the coupled joints cannot implement this ownership partition directly.

docs.title: Supported model scope
docs.text:
The validated partition covers fixed-base robots where every independently actuated coordinate is owned by AUGUR. The external simulator owns the links and environmental dynamics, but it does not contain another motor, drive, transmission, or forward-integrated state for those coordinates.

Floating-base robots and mixed coordinate ownership require a coupled solve. For example, if the simulator owns a free base while AUGUR owns the joints, base acceleration, contact reactions, and actuator loads depend on each other. Stepping the simulator and then overwriting the actuator joints does not solve that system consistently.

Compliant transmissions, stiff impacts, closed-loop mechanisms, and other strongly constrained systems may also require model-specific coupling and stability work.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Validate each robot model and coupling implementation with:

  1. no-load motion matching the standalone AUGUR actuator;
  2. joint-load direction and magnitude checks;
  3. constant external torque tests;
  4. trajectory convergence as the exchange rate increases, we recommends starting from >= 500hz, but depends on the platform and trajectories;
  5. bounded uncommanded energy and passive behavior;
  6. multi-joint cross-inertial coupling;
  7. finite contact loads, bounded penetration, and converging contact trajectories;
  8. joint-limit and collision behavior.

A useful starting sweep is 100, 200, 500, and 1,000 Hz. Passing these checks confirms the implementation for the tested mechanism and operating range.

See Robot modelling for constructing the external robot model in URDF, MJCF, SDF, OpenUSD, or another simulator format.

docs.title: Robot modelling
docs.text: This page describes how to build external robot models for co-simulation use between rigid-body simulators and AUGUR virtual actuators. Read the co-simulation coupling first for more information; the models described here supplies the robot dynamics used to calculate each actuator's load.

docs.title: Model one actuator-driven joint
docs.text:
Represent each PULSE actuator as one revolute robot joint between a parent link and a child link:

parent link ── revolute joint ── child link
                    │
                    └── one PulsarActuatorVirtual

The joint coordinate must describe the actuator output shaft directly:

  • angle in radians;
  • angular velocity in radians per second;
  • joint effort in N·m;
  • double check the joint axis and positive direction matching the AUGUR actuator;
  • gear ratio of 1 at the coupling boundary, because AUGUR already reports output-shaft state and accounts internally for transmission and its effects.

Give every coupled joint a stable name and map it to one virtual actuator address in the integration code.

docs.title: Divide the physical properties correctly
docs.text:
The external model should -depending on the format- include:

  • the mass, center of mass, and inertia of every robot link;
  • actuator housing and structural mass assigned to the link that carries it;
  • downstream brackets, output flanges, tools, and payloads assigned to the appropriate link;
  • any mechanism-level damping, springs, or friction not represented by AUGUR, like external bearings, belt drive, linkages, etc;
  • visual and collision geometry;
  • environmental contacts and constraints.

Do not add duplicate motor or transmission model to an AUGUR-owned joint. In particular, do not duplicate:

  • motor rotor inertia;
  • reflected gearbox inertia;
  • drivetrain friction;
  • a torque, position, velocity, or impedance drive;
  • simulator armature added for the virtual actuator.

docs.title: Build a multi-joint robot
docs.text:
For a serial robot, repeat the same pattern for each degree of freedom:

base ─ joint_1 ─ link_1 ─ joint_2 ─ link_2 ─ ... ─ joint_n ─ link_n
          │                    │                              │
       AUGUR 1              AUGUR 2                        AUGUR n

Each independently actuated revolute joint needs:

  1. one joint coordinate in the robot model;
  2. one PulsarActuatorVirtual in the shared VirtualWorld;
  3. one joint-name-to-actuator-address mapping;
  4. the same zero position and positive direction in both systems.

Dependent joints, mimic joints, tendons, closed loops, and compliant transmissions need an explicit constraint or transmission model. Do not assign an independent AUGUR virtual actuator to a dependent coordinate unless the physical robot actually has one there, which is very unlikely, but for example an AUGUR actuator connected to a rod that is also actuated by a linear motor, both will see the dependant motion as load and will result in undefined behavior.

docs.title: Common model checklist
docs.text:
Before choosing a file format, define:

Property What to provide Link frames A consistent parent-to-child frame convention Joint origin Position and orientation of the output shaft relative to the parent link Joint axis Unit axis with the same positive direction as AUGUR Joint limits Physical lower, upper, velocity, and effort limits where supported Link inertia Mass, center of mass, and a valid positive-definite inertia tensor Collision geometry Simple, stable shapes where possible Visual geometry Optional detailed meshes, separate from collision meshes Passive mechanics Only effects outside the AUGUR drivetrain model Simulator drive None on an AUGUR-owned joint

Start with a single joint and no contact. Add the remaining links, then gravity, and contacts only after the basic joint mapping is correct.

Simulator Typical input MuJoCo MJCF; URDF can be imported and inspected Gazebo SDF or URDF Newton URDF, MJCF, or OpenUSD Other simulators Their native format or a verified URDF/MJCF/OpenUSD importer MuJoCoGazeboNewtonOther Simulators

MuJoCo's default format is MJCF, but also accepts import and translation of URDF and OpenUSD (experimental). MJCF represents a robot through nested bodies. A minimal hinge joint has this structure:

<mujoco model="augur_robot">
  <compiler angle="radian"/>
  <worldbody>
    <body name="base">
      <body name="link_1" pos="0 0 0">
        <joint name="joint_1" type="hinge" axis="0 0 1"
               range="-1.57 1.57" armature="0"/>
        <inertial pos="0 0 0.1" mass="2.0"
                  diaginertia="0.02 0.02 0.01"/>
        <geom type="mesh" mesh="link_1_visual" contype="0" conaffinity="0"/>
        <geom type="capsule" size="0.04 0.2"/>
      </body>
    </body>
  </worldbody>
</mujoco>

For an AUGUR-owned joint:

  • use a hinge joint whose axis and reference position match AUGUR, or invert the direction inside PulsarActuatorVirtual;
  • keep armature="0" unless it represents mechanism inertia not already in AUGUR;
  • omit an entry for that joint from the MJCF <actuator> section;
  • use joint damping, friction loss, and springs only for passive mechanism effects outside the actuator model;
  • keep detailed visual meshes separate from simpler collision geometry where practical.

URDF import can provide an initial MuJoCo model, but inspect the converted inertias, joint ranges, mesh scales, and any generated actuator or armature settings before using it for co-simulation. MuJoCo had previously had issues with importing inertias correctly from URDF especially if they use diagnoal not the full inertia values, its worth a double check if you're seeing unexpected behavior.

Gazebo work primarily with URDF and SDF formats. URDF represents a robot as links connected by joints. A minimal actuator-driven revolute joint has this structure:

<link name="base"/>

<link name="link_1">
  <inertial>
    <origin xyz="0 0 0.1" rpy="0 0 0"/>
    <mass value="2.0"/>
    <inertia ixx="0.02" ixy="0" ixz="0"
             iyy="0.02" iyz="0" izz="0.01"/>
  </inertial>
  <visual>...</visual>
  <collision>...</collision>
</link>

<joint name="joint_1" type="revolute">
  <parent link="base"/>
  <child link="link_1"/>
  <origin xyz="0 0 0" rpy="0 0 0"/>
  <axis xyz="0 0 1"/>
</joint>

For an AUGUR-owned joint:

  • use revolute for a limited joint or continuous for an unlimited rotary joint;
  • make the URDF axis match the actuator's positive output direction or you can simply invert the direction in the PulsarActuatorVirtual class;
  • omit transmissions and controller plugins that apply effort to that joint;
  • avoid joint damping or friction values that duplicate actuator drivetrain losses. you can add them if you physcially have extra mechanisms that physically add this behavior in addition to the actuator internals, such as bearings, springs, belt drives, etc.

Gazebo can consume URDF or SDF. In SDF, create the equivalent model, link, and joint elements and leave the coupled joint without a competing drive plugin. Use Gazebo-specific sensors, contact parameters, and environment definitions only for effects that belong to the robot or world model.

Newton can work with several formats since it has many internal solvers (including MuJoCo for rigid body), so it can support MJCF, but it is recommended to use OpenUSD to work seamlessly with the other solvers.

In OpenUSD, represent the robot as a rigid-body articulation:

  1. create one rigid body for each link;
  2. assign mass properties and collision geometry to each body;
  3. connect parent and child bodies with a revolute physics joint;
  4. set the joint frames, axis, and limits to match the actuator output shaft;
  5. apply the articulation schema expected by the target simulator;
  6. do not apply a joint drive schema to an AUGUR-owned joint.

Newton can build a model from URDF, MJCF, or OpenUSD. Whichever source is used, verify the resulting articulation, joint axes, inertias, collision shapes, units, and drive settings after import. Prefer a native OpenUSD representation when an importer cannot preserve those properties reliably.

The same model structure applies to another simulator or native format:

  • rigid links carry mass and inertia;
  • revolute joints define the AUGUR output coordinates;
  • the environment supplies gravity, contacts, and constraints;
  • no second actuator drives an AUGUR-owned joint.

A file format being accepted by a simulator does not guarantee that the simulator exposes the state-imposition and inverse-dynamics operations required by the coupling. Confirm those capabilities before investing in a detailed model.

docs.title: Verify the model before coupling
docs.text:
Check the robot model independently:

  1. link masses and centers of mass match the intended mechanism;
  2. inertia tensors are valid and expressed in the correct frames;
  3. joint axes, zeros, limits, and mesh scales are correct;
  4. collision shapes do not begin in penetration;
  5. gravity produces the expected joint-load direction and approximate magnitude;
  6. no hidden drive, transmission, armature, or duplicated drivetrain loss remains, including the default values of each simulator since some inject base damping values to stabelize their solvers;
  7. a single-joint inverse-dynamics test agrees with expected result or a hand calculation.

Then apply the convergence, energy, multi-joint, limit, and contact tips from Co-simulation coupling.

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
PULSE actuators provide four user-facing control modes. The physical firmware and AUGUR Digital Twin models run the same low-level control algorithms at 20 kHz.

Mode Pulsar Python SDK enum Primary command Torque control Mode.TORQUE torque in N·m Speed/velocity control Mode.VELOCITY angular velocity in rad/s Position control Mode.POSITION output position in rad Impedance control Mode.IMPEDANCE position in rad plus optional impedance fields

Pulsar App labels velocity mode as Speed Control. Pulsar Python SDK uses the more precise enum name VELOCITY.

docs.title: Torque
docs.text: The command is converted to field-oriented current references and regulated by the motor current loop, subject to configured limits.

docs.title: Velocity
docs.text: An outer proportional-integral velocity loop produces the torque request for the inner torque/current control loop.

docs.title: Position
docs.text: An outer position controller generates a velocity request for the nested velocity and torque loops.

docs.title: Impedance
docs.text:
Virtual stiffness, damping, inertia, and feedforward terms produce a compliant torque request from position and velocity behavior.

For valid command fields and persistent parameters, continue with Control parameters by mode.

docs.title: Regenerative energy management
docs.text:
TL;DR

PULSAR actuators can return energy to the DC bus during braking. Provide an appropriate way to absorb this energy when designing the power system, and monitor bus voltage during operation.

A conventional 48 V Power Supply Unit (PSU) is not necessarily able to absorb returned energy but should be enable to start running conservative tests at a minimum. Any initial testing must be assessed for the complete system: start with small, slow movements, monitor bus voltage, and increase dynamics gradually. The specific research tests documented below completed on a 4dof with conventional PSU without any observed damage, including for very high dynamics as shown; this is not assurance for other setups.

PULSAR QDD actuators operate from a nominal 48 V DC supply. In a multi-actuator system, they are often connected to a shared DC bus, depending on the system power architecture.

The actuators use quasi-direct drive (QDD) transmissions with low reduction ratios, making them highly backdrivable. During deceleration or externally driven motion, the motor can act as a generator and return electrical energy to the DC bus. The bus voltage then depends on what the other actuators consume, what the supply or battery can absorb, and whether the system has a braking path.

This page explains power-up, bus-voltage behavior, and practical ways to manage regeneration. The numerical values below refer to the PULSE115-60G and provide general, initial guidelines.

Check the specifications and firmware settings applicable to your actuator and system.

See Electrical Interfaces for the 48 V power connector and general bus requirements.

docs.title: DC-bus characteristics and power-up
docs.text:
Characteristic PULSE115-60G value or behavior Nominal supply 48 V DC Total nominal input capacitance Approximately 163 µF per actuator Equivalent capacitor ESR Approximately 700 µΩ Built-in precharge or active inrush limiting None Undervoltage / overvoltage fault limits 30 V / 60 V, preset in firmware and not user configurable Control electronics power Supplied from the same 48 V input; no separate logic input Typical disabled current Approximately 100 mA Typical enabled current at zero command, with no active control Approximately 150 mA

Safety

Regenerated energy can raise the DC-bus voltage. Do not assume a conventional supply can absorb current, and do not treat the test results on this page as a system rating or guarantee. Use a suitable energy-management path and monitor the bus during staged testing.

Precharge external switched power rails. Connecting an uncharged actuator directly to a stiff source can produce an inrush transient. A peak current and duration for direct, uncontrolled connection have not been characterized. A connector with an anti-spark resistor, such as the XT90-S used in some system builds, helps during manual connection; it is not a replacement for a designed precharge path in a relay-switched distribution board.

For an illustrative 48 V rail, a 1.8 kΩ series precharge resistor and a single actuator's nominal 163 µF input capacitance give:

  • Initial current: I₀ ≈ 48 V / 1.8 kΩ = 26.7 mA.
  • Ideal time constant: τ = RC ≈ 0.293 s.

In the ideal RC model, five time constants are about 1.47 s and bring the capacitor to approximately 99.3% of the source voltage. The resistor initially dissipates approximately 1.28 W, then less as charging proceeds.

These are estimates, not a validated relay-bypass delay or resistor rating. Size the pulse-energy and power rating for the actual source, wiring, number of actuators, and repeated connection cycle; confirm the actuator-side bus voltage before closing the bypass.

Additional bus capacitance and electronics powered during precharge can change the measured charge time. The capacitor stores approximately 0.19 J at 48 V, so its capacitance alone should not be treated as a sustained braking-energy sink.

Removing 48 V turns off the actuator, including its control electronics. Allow the internal capacitors to discharge safely before reconnecting power.

This information does not establish a specific CAN/USB connection order or automatic restart behavior after a power interruption; validate the intended sequence in the complete system.

docs.title: What happens during braking
docs.text:
When mechanical energy drives the motor, electrical power can flow back through its drive to the shared DC bus. An individual joint can regenerate while the whole arm still consumes power: other joints and electronics can use the returned energy locally.

If the total returned power exceeds the loads' consumption and the supply cannot sink current, the bus voltage can rise. A one-quadrant bench supply generally sources current but should not be assumed to absorb returned current.

As of the end of 2026, our actuators have no built-in brake chopper or braking resistor. Design the external power system so regenerative energy has a suitable destination, such as:

  • A supply explicitly rated to sink the expected current and energy.
  • An external, voltage-controlled brake chopper with a correctly sized braking resistor.
  • A battery and battery-management path rated to accept the returned charge under the actual state-of-charge, temperature, and fault conditions.
  • Other actuators or loads on the same bus, where their concurrent consumption is verified for the operating envelope. Shared loads may reduce the net returned energy, but are not a guaranteed sink at every instant.

Select the braking turn-on level and protective limits using the whole system's wiring and transient response. The actuator's fault limits set in firmware are 30 V and 60 V for the PULSE115-60G.

Voltage warnings have also been described around the 45 V and 53 V boundaries; the exact warning behavior, hysteresis, sampling point, and recovery conditions should be checked for the installed firmware. Do not use a warning indication as the sole design margin for a brake chopper.

If a voltage-related fault appears while an external meter reports a lower peak bus voltage, capture the bus voltage at the actuator terminals with adequate bandwidth and correlate it with the drive's fault record. A slow measurement at the PSU can miss a local or brief excursion, and the available values alone do not establish the fault's cause.

For example, an observed rise from 48.2 V to 52.2 V over 0.2 s during approximately 35 W of braking does not by itself demonstrate that the documented 60 V overvoltage limit was reached. Confirm the particular fault condition before changing the power architecture.

docs.title: Pulse Arm 4DOF: measured dynamic example
docs.text:
An appropriate way to absorb regenerated energy is recommended when designing the power system. In our experience, conventional power supplies can also support initial testing and non-extreme operation without a dedicated regeneration system.

We have extensively tested platforms built with our actuators using many power supplies, from expensive laboratory units to inexpensive hobby-level models, as well as batteries. In our internal testing to date, we have not damaged an actuator or power supply during operation, including tests with aggressive dynamics like the fast trajectory shown below.

Start with small, slow movements and gradually increase the operating range and dynamics while observing actuator behavior and the DC bus voltage. Assess the specific power source, loads, wiring, and motion before increasing speed or acceleration.

Regenerative behavior depends on the complete system, so our experience does not guarantee the same outcome in every setup.

Disclaimer: PULSAR HRI is not liable for damage to power electronics resulting from the use of this guidance or the operation of a system without a dedicated means of managing regenerated energy.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
The following example uses a four-joint Pulse Arm with 2 × PULSE115-60G and 2 × PULSE98-30G actuators on a shared 48 V bus. The supply used for these experiments was an EA-PS 9200-25 T, 1500 W.

The high-level controller streams a precomputed joint-position trajectory at 100 Hz, open loop at the arm level, without gravity compensation or other high-level feedback. Each actuator runs its local position control at 20 kHz, with joint-level control gains set using the digital twin and empirical testing to achieve adequate tracking without instability.

Joint Actuator model POSITION_KP VELOCITY_KP VELOCITY_KI J1 PULSE115-60G 16.0 0.6 3.0 J2 PULSE115-60G 16.0 0.6 4.0 J3 PULSE98-30G 16.0 0.2 6.4 J4 PULSE98-30G 16.0 0.4 6.4

The gains are the values used for this experiment; suitable gains depend on the actuator model, payload, and system dynamics.

The 100 Hz CAN stream sends joint position commands from the central computing unit (a standard laptop), while each actuator executes its local cascaded position and FOC current loops at 20 kHz (POSITION control mode). For an overview of control modes available on the actuators, see Control.

In the joint power plots, positive power indicates electrical consumption (motoring), while negative power indicates electrical regeneration (braking). The plotted joint traces represent the instantaneous aggregate electrical power per actuator (Pelec = 3/2 (v_d i_d + v_q i_q), computed onboard at 20 kHz from measured shunt currents and commanded dq voltages, then streamed at 100 Hz as BUS_POWER). They do not represent individual raw AC phase waveforms.

Total energy from the joint plots should not be directly equated with external bench PSU measurements. Joint telemetry captures motor electromechanical conversion and excludes the ~3–5 W per-actuator baseline electronics consumption. The PSU is sampled at a lower rate (10 Hz vs. 100 Hz), and its logging window spans the entire run rather than the segmented trajectory window.

docs.title: Fast, aggressive trajectory
docs.text:
The fast run, identified as y_axis/accel_40p0/v_max_2p0, produces repeated reversals, with some joints returning energy while others draw it. The joint-power window is 1.84 s long.

The plot reports a 97 W peak draw, a 37 W peak regenerative magnitude, 69.3 J of gross positive energy, 14.2 J of gross returned energy, and 55.0 J net positive energy. Its reported regenerative fraction, 20.5%, is 14.2 J divided by 69.3 J for this window; it is not an end-to-end energy-recovery efficiency.

Fast run, joint-side power. The black line is the total of the joint traces; green shading marks intervals when its sign is regenerative. Power and energy values are specific to the displayed 1.84 s window.

The one-quadrant PSU remained a net source in this example. Its plotted voltage ranges from 47.94 V to 48.61 V, and its supply-side power peaks at 68.55 W.

The plot reports 397.84 J over its full approximately 16 s record, including the idle periods before and after the movement. Its current trace stays positive at the displayed resolution.

Those observations are consistent with regenerated energy being used elsewhere on the shared bus or temporarily stored, but they do not measure the precise destination of each returned joule.

Fast run, PSU-side voltage, current, and power. The green and red vertical lines mark the execution window in the full recording.

The test completed on a standard one-quadrant supply without observed damage to the supply or actuators. This is a result for this configuration and motion, not a guarantee for a different trajectory, load, bus capacitance, or supply.

docs.title: Slow comparison trajectory
docs.text:
The slow run is identified as y_axis/accel_40p0/v_max_0p1. In the 27.01 s joint-power window, the plot reports 54.5 J drawn, 0.9 J regenerated, 53.6 J net energy and a 1.7% regenerative fraction.

Peak draw is shown rounded to 4 W, and peak regeneration is shown rounded to 0 W. Individual joint traces briefly go negative while the total arm trace remains positive at the displayed resolution.

The longer window means its energy totals should not be compared directly with the fast run's 1.84 s window.

Slow run, signed joint power and total arm power.

The PSU plot reports a 47.95 V bus throughout the recording at its displayed precision, a 22.05 W peak supply power and 874.23 J over the full approximately 41.5 s recording. Most supply power remains close to the idle level during the motion.

The supply-side energy includes idle periods and is measured over a different window from the joint plot.

Slow run, PSU voltage, current, and power over the complete recording.

The slow trajectory shows substantially lower peak joint power and a smaller reported regenerative fraction than the fast trajectory in these recordings. The tests have different durations, so compare power and the plotted time histories rather than total energy alone.

For both trajectories, compare the sign and timing of joint power with the PSU voltage and current, including the supply's idle draw. A negative joint-power interval does not imply negative PSU current if other bus loads consume that power. Confirm the same sensor locations, power definitions, sample rates, and time alignment before comparing magnitudes.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
In these Pulse Arm tests, the slow trajectory produced a much smaller regenerative fraction and lower peak power than the aggressive trajectory. The conventional power supply remained a net source during the displayed recordings, and no damage was observed in these tests.

These results illustrate a practical starting point, rather than a limit for other systems. Start slowly, monitor the bus voltage, and increase motion dynamics gradually. Select a suitable means of absorbing regenerated energy for the operating conditions of the complete system.

docs.title: Safety and prerequisites
docs.text: Hardware

docs.title: Safety and prerequisites
docs.text: PULSE actuators can move quickly and produce substantial torque. Treat every connected actuator as capable of immediate motion.

docs.title: Before applying power
docs.text:
• Secure the actuator to a fixture or robot structure suitable for the expected load.
  • Keep the output and attached mechanism clear of people, cables, tools, and loose objects.
  • Confirm the power supply voltage, current capacity, polarity, and connector wiring.
  • Provide a reliable way to remove power.
  • Check mechanical travel, collisions, and cable strain before enabling drive output.

docs.title: Before running software
docs.text:
• Use firmware 2.0.4 or newer with Pulsar SDK.
  • Start with conservative commands, gains, limits, and telemetry rates.
  • Set the current position as zero only when the resulting reference is understood.
  • Do not change control parameters in large jumps while the actuator is active.
  • For CAN FD, verify unique addresses and termination at both physical ends of the bus.

docs.title: Safe software lifecycle
docs.text:
With Pulsar Python SDK:

  1. connect;
  2. configure while output is inactive;
  3. enable only when the mechanism is clear;
  4. send bounded commands;
  5. disable before reconfiguration or shutdown;
  6. disconnect or exit the context manager.

Do not rely on garbage collection or process exit as a hardware stop mechanism.

Warning

Software safety actions are best effort when communication is lost. If an actuator is unreachable, the SDK reports its state as unknown rather than claiming that it is safe.

docs.text: Hardware

docs.title: CAN FD
docs.text: CAN FD connects one or more PULSE actuators to a computer through a USB-to-CAN adapter.

docs.title: Required hardware
docs.text:
• one Pulsar USB-to-CAN adapter;
  • one USB cable for the adapter;
  • CAN cables with compatible 3-pin Molex PicoBlade connectors;
  • one CAN-Terminator at each physical end of the bus;
  • powered, securely mounted actuators with unique addresses.

See Electrical interfaces for connector and pinout details.

docs.title: Wire one actuator
docs.text:
1. Connect the adapter to the computer.
  2. Put one CAN-Terminator on one adapter CAN port.
  3. Connect the other adapter CAN port to either actuator CAN port.
  4. Put the second CAN-Terminator on the actuator's unused CAN port.

CAN ports are bidirectional. The CAN-Terminators must remain at the two physical ends of the complete bus.

docs.title: Discover addresses
docs.text:
Install Pulsar Python SDK, then scan the bus:

pulsar-cli scan

The default scan range is 16–255. Valid actuator CAN addresses are 16–16382.

docs.title: Add actuators
docs.text:
Daisy-chain additional actuators and keep only two CAN-Terminators, one at each physical end. Every actuator on one PcpOverCan domain must have a unique address.

More than eight registered actuators is allowed, but is not recommended for stability and to get the most performance. Request only the telemetry required by the application and use the CAN bus utilization tool to estimate your utilization before increasing actuator count or rates.

docs.title: Planning multiple buses
docs.text:
Actuators on one CAN FD bus share its communication capacity. For larger systems, consider distributing actuators across independent buses, each with its own compatible USB-to-CAN adapter, subject to host USB-port availability. Plan each bus separately for command and telemetry traffic, physical wiring, and electrical loading.

Use the CAN bus utilization tool to estimate communication utilization. This estimate does not establish electrical compatibility or guarantee real-time performance. Each independent bus must retain termination at both physical ends; see Wire one actuator for the termination arrangement.

The shown node count and addresses are examples, not a product limit. The exposed adapter board is shown for identification only; do not remove an enclosure or operate a board unenclosed to avoid interference at high communication speeds.

docs.title: Data-rate switching
docs.text: CAN FD can use a 5 Mbit/s data phase. Treat bit-rate switching as a bus-wide configuration: all devices on the bus must be compatible and configured consistently.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Continue with the CAN FD quickstart or the Pulsar Python SDK physical-CAN guide for software setup.

docs.title: Adapter not detected
docs.text:
• reconnect the adapter;
  • try another USB cable or port;
  • pass the serial port explicitly;
  • check operating-system serial permissions.

docs.title: No actuator found
docs.text:
• confirm actuator power;
  • check CAN_H, CAN_L, and ground wiring;
  • verify both CAN-Terminators;
  • try a smaller scan range around known addresses;
  • replace worn-out cables.

If the problem persists, contact support.

docs.title: CAN bus utilization
docs.text: Hardware

docs.title: CAN bus utilization
docs.text:
Estimate the theoretical CAN FD load for a group of PULSE actuators. Adjust actuator count, telemetry selection, command rate, and data bitrate before configuring a high-rate system.

Actuators 6 1–10 actuators on one bus Telemetry items per actuator 4 Each item uses a 1-byte identifier and a 4-byte value Telemetry frequency Hz Sent by each actuator Command frequency Hz Sent by the host to each actuator Control mode Torque Velocity Position Impedance Determines the maximum command parameters Command parameters 8 / 8 Includes the command; each parameter is a float32 CAN FD data bitrate 1 Mbit/s 5 Mbit/s

docs.title: Estimated utilization
docs.text: 0.0% of bus capacity Telemetry0.0% Commands0.0% Telemetry frame— Command frame— Total frames—

docs.title: Calculation
docs.text:
Each telemetry item occupies five data bytes: a one-byte identifier and a four-byte value. Payloads are rounded to a valid CAN FD size. Pulsar Python SDK permits at most 12 configured telemetry items.

Each command contains an action identifier followed by mode-specific float32 values. The estimate includes extended identifiers, protocol overhead, inter-frame spacing, and worst-case bit stuffing.

Note

This is a theoretical upper-bound estimate. Leave headroom for arbitration, configuration, diagnostics, retransmissions, clock tolerance, adapter timing, and other non-periodic traffic. A value below 100% is not a real-time guarantee.

docs.title: Physical actuator over direct USB with Pulsar App (browser)
docs.text: This is the fastest way to move one physical PULSE actuator without writing code.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• one securely mounted PULSE actuator;
  • a suitable 48 V DC power supply and power cable;
  • a USB-A to USB-C cable;
  • Chrome or another Chromium-based browser on Linux or Windows.

Read Safety and prerequisites before continuing.

docs.title: Connect the actuator
docs.text:
1. Mount the actuator so it cannot move unexpectedly as a whole.
  2. Connect the power cable and switch on the power supply.
  3. Confirm that the status LED turns on.
  4. Connect the actuator directly to the computer by USB.
  5. Confirm that the LED indicates a USB connection.

docs.title: Open Pulsar App
docs.text:
1. Open https://app.pulsarhri.com/.
  2. Allow the browser to access the connected serial device.
  3. Select the actuator in Devices. Use refresh if it is not listed.

Warning

Once connected and enabled, commands can cause immediate motion. Keep people, cables, tools, and loose objects outside the operating area.

docs.title: Try velocity control
docs.text:
1. Select Speed Control.
  2. Confirm that the setpoint is 0 rad/s.
  3. Press Play.
  4. Increase the setpoint gradually and observe the actuator and live plot.
  5. Return the setpoint to zero before changing mode.

docs.title: Try position control
docs.text:
1. Select Position Control.
  2. Press SET 0 POSITION to use the current output position as zero.
  3. Press Play while the setpoint is zero.
  4. Change the position setpoint by a small amount and observe the response.

Change gains and limits only in small increments. A gain that is too high can produce overshoot or unstable motion.

docs.title: Prepare the bus
docs.text:
Before writing code:

  1. securely mount and power every actuator;
  2. wire the CAN bus with CAN termination at both physical ends;
  3. connect the Pulsar USB-to-CAN adapter;
  4. confirm that every actuator has a unique address using pulsar-cli;
  5. read CAN FD connectivity.

docs.title: Find actuator addresses
docs.text:
After installing Pulsar Python SDK, scan the bus:

With one connected Pulsar device:

pixi run pulsar-cli scan

With several connected devices, select the adapter port:

LinuxWindows PowerShell 
pixi run pulsar-cli scan --port /dev/ttyACM0

pixi run pulsar-cli scan --port COM3

Replace the example port with the exact port on your machine.

docs.title: Configure one group
docs.text:
Replace the example addresses below with the values reported by the scan.

from time import sleep

from pulsar_sdk import (
    ActuatorGroup,
    ControlConfiguration,
    ControlParams,
    Mode,
    PcpOverCan,
    PulsarActuatorReal,
)

can = PcpOverCan()
arm = ActuatorGroup(
    "arm",
    {
        "shoulder": PulsarActuatorReal(can, address=23),
        "elbow": PulsarActuatorReal(can, address=24),
    },
)

with arm:
    arm.configure(ControlConfiguration(Mode.VELOCITY))
    arm.enable()
    arm.set_commands({
        "shoulder": {ControlParams.COMMAND: 0.2},
        "elbow": {ControlParams.COMMAND: -0.2},
    })
    sleep(2)
    arm.disable()

PcpOverCan() automatically selects the port when only one Pulsar CAN Adapter is connected. With several adapters, use PcpOverCan.list_ports() and construct the domain as PcpOverCan(chosen_port).

The SDK validates the complete selected batch before the first write. Member writes are still sequential, so a later transport failure can occur after an earlier actuator was updated.

docs.title: Install with Pixi
docs.text:
Pixi creates a reproducible project environment and uses the same project commands on Linux and Windows.

pixi init pulsar-quickstart
cd pulsar-quickstart
pixi workspace channel add --prepend https://prefix.dev/pulsarhri/pulsar-forge
pixi add pulsar-sdk

docs.title: Run a short velocity command
docs.text:
Create quickstart.py:

from time import sleep

from pulsar_sdk import (
    ControlConfiguration,
    Mode,
    PulsarActuatorReal,
    TelemetryItems,
    PcpOverUsb,
)

usb = PcpOverUsb()
actuator = PulsarActuatorReal(usb, address=0)

with actuator:
    actuator.configure(
        ControlConfiguration(
            mode=Mode.VELOCITY,
            telemetry_items=(
                TelemetryItems.POSITION,
                TelemetryItems.VELOCITY,
            ),
            telemetry_rate_hz=100,
        )
    )
    actuator.enable()
    actuator.set_command(1.0)  # rad/s

    sleep(2)

    print(actuator.read_telemetry((
        TelemetryItems.POSITION,
        TelemetryItems.VELOCITY,
    )))
    actuator.disable()

Run it inside the project environment:

pixi run python quickstart.py

The context manager connects before the body and disconnects when the body exits. disable() turns drive output off while keeping runtime telemetry available until disconnect.

Danger

Do not rely on Python object destruction to stop hardware. Use disable() and disconnect(), preferably through a context manager as shown above.

docs.text: Run a PULSE115-60G virtual actuator using AUGUR Digital Twin assets. No physical actuator, power supply, USB cable, or CAN adapter is required.

docs.title: Install the SDK and assets
docs.text:
Install Pixi first, then create a pixi project environment.

pixi init pulsar-virtual-quickstart
cd pulsar-virtual-quickstart
pixi workspace channel add --prepend https://prefix.dev/pulsarhri/pulsar-forge
pixi add pulsar-sdk pulsar-assets

License notice

pulsar-assets and AUGUR Digital Twin operate under the AUGUR Development Licence (ADL) and AUGUR Commercial License (ACL). Read the AUGUR license before using the digital twins.

Check the installed models:

pixi run pulsar-cli vscan # or virtual-scan, vs

docs.title: Run the virtual actuator
docs.text:
Create virtual_quickstart.py:

from pulsar_sdk import (
    ControlConfiguration,
    Mode,
    PulsarActuatorVirtual,
    TelemetryItems,
    VirtualWorld,
)

world = VirtualWorld()
actuator = PulsarActuatorVirtual(
    world,
    model="PULSE115-60G",
    address=1,
)

with actuator:
    actuator.configure(
        ControlConfiguration(
            mode=Mode.VELOCITY,
            telemetry_items=(
                TelemetryItems.POSITION,
                TelemetryItems.VELOCITY,
            ),
            telemetry_rate_hz=100,
        )
    )
    actuator.enable()
    actuator.set_command(1.0)

    for _ in range(10):
        world.step()

    print(actuator.read_telemetry((
        TelemetryItems.POSITION,
        TelemetryItems.VELOCITY,
    )))
    actuator.disable()

Run it:

pixi run python virtual_quickstart.py

VirtualWorld.step() advances to the next periodic telemetry event and waits for due callbacks. If periodic telemetry is disabled, each call advances one 50 µs model tick.

docs.title: ExecutionDomain
docs.text:
ExecutionDomain(*, logger: logging.Logger | None = None)

Base class for one transport or simulation clock. It also owns the callback worker, telemetry watchdog, and actuator leases.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• capabilities: Capability
  • connection_state: ConnectionState
  • is_connected: bool

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
• supports(capability: Capability) -> bool — Return whether the domain advertises the capability.
  • connect() -> None — Explicitly keep the domain open. Repeated calls are safe.
  • disconnect() -> None — Release the explicit connection. Raises ResourceBusyError while connected actuators still use the domain.
  • sync() -> FeatureResult — Reset telemetry timestamps and counters for the domain when supported.
  • reset_telemetry_timestamp() -> FeatureResult — Same operation as sync().

The class supports with; entering connects and exiting disconnects.

docs.title: PcpOverCan
docs.text:
PcpOverCan(
    port: str | None = None,
    *,
    logger: logging.Logger | None = None,
)

PCP domain for one USB-to-CAN adapter.

  • list_ports() -> tuple[str, ...] — List detected Pulsar serial ports.
  • scan(start_address=16, end_address=255, *, timeout_s=0.12) -> tuple[int, ...] — Probe the inclusive address range. The domain connects automatically if needed.
  • set_can_brs_enabled(enabled: bool) -> None — Update connected actuators while output is inactive. Enabling BRS is verified and rolled back on failure.

CAN actuator addresses must be unique within the domain and lie in 16..16382. Scan bounds use the same range, start_address must not exceed end_address, and timeout_s must be finite and positive.

Backend-neutral actuator contract. Most users create PulsarActuatorReal or PulsarActuatorVirtual instead.

diagnostic_actions maps named DiagnosticFlag values to safety actions. Defaults are:

  • DiagnosticFlag.OVERTEMPERATURE → LIMIT_TORQUE
  • DiagnosticFlag.INTERNAL_ENCODER_ERROR and EXTERNAL_ENCODER_ERROR → INIT_CONFIG
  • other unmapped error diagnostics → DEFAULT_SAFETY

Map a diagnostic to DO_NOTHING to keep it report-only: callbacks and status.diagnostic still update, but it does not fault, inhibit, pause, propagate safety, or block direct commands/enabling. Mapping every DiagnosticFlag provides the explicit destructive-testing configuration.

diagnostic_damping must be None or a finite positive value.

Physical actuator using Pulsar Communication Protocols (PCP).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter reads are backend-specific. Writes are allowed only while drive output is inactive.

These values are directly writable with set_parameters():

  • impedance gains: IMPEDANCE_DAMPING, IMPEDANCE_STIFFNESS;
  • torque, position, velocity, profile-velocity, and profile-acceleration limits;
  • loop gains: VELOCITY_KP, VELOCITY_KI, POSITION_KP, FEEDFORWARD_GAIN;
  • DIRECTION_INVERTED, VELOCITY_FILTER_CUTOFF, CURRENT_FILTER_CUTOFF, and CAN_BRS_ENABLED.

The following values require dedicated methods instead:

  • MODE → set_mode();
  • COMMAND → command methods;
  • TORQUE_GAIN_PRESET and VELOCITY_GAIN_PRESET → preset methods;
  • PCP_ADDRESS → set_address();
  • TELEMETRY_RATE_HZ → configure().

These fields are read-only: RATED_VELOCITY_RAD_S, MAXIMUM_TORQUE_NM, FIRMWARE_VERSION, SERIAL_NUMBER, DEVICE_MODEL, and CONTROL_MODEL_CRC. A backend may reject an otherwise writable field that its device or model does not provide.

docs.title: Command-line interface
docs.text:
Installing Pulsar Python SDK provides pulsar-cli in the active environment.

With Pixi, prefix commands with pixi run:

pixi run pulsar-cli --help

Commands without a serial port are identical on Linux and Windows. Where a port is required, use the platform-specific form shown below.

docs.title: Scan a CAN bus
docs.text:
The CLI automatically uses the adapter when exactly one Pulsar serial device is connected:

pulsar-cli scan

Select a port when several devices are connected:

LinuxWindows PowerShell 
pulsar-cli scan --port /dev/ttyACM0

pulsar-cli scan --port COM3

Optional bounds accept decimal or hexadecimal integers:

pulsar-cli scan --begin 0x10 --end 0x40 --timeout 0.12

docs.title: Scan virtual assets
docs.text:
pulsar-cli virtual-scan

Aliases: vscan, vs.

docs.title: Read parameters
docs.text:
Direct USB:

pulsar-cli params

CAN:

LinuxWindows PowerShell 
pulsar-cli params --port /dev/ttyACM0 --address 16

pulsar-cli params --port COM3 --address 16

docs.title: Identify an actuator
docs.text:
LinuxWindows PowerShell 
pulsar-cli blink --port /dev/ttyACM0 --address 16

pulsar-cli blink --port COM3 --address 16

docs.title: Zero the current position
docs.text:
Direct USB:

pulsar-cli home

CAN:

LinuxWindows PowerShell 
pulsar-cli home --port /dev/ttyACM0 --address 0x10

pulsar-cli home --port COM3 --address 0x10

The CLI enters CONFIG_AND_TELEM before requesting the zero operation.

docs.title: Change a CAN address
docs.text:
LinuxWindows PowerShell 
pulsar-cli change-address --port /dev/ttyACM0 NEW_ADDRESS CURRENT_ADDRESS

pulsar-cli change-address --port COM3 NEW_ADDRESS CURRENT_ADDRESS

Direct-USB address changes are unsupported.

Run pulsar-cli <command> --help for exact options.

docs.text: Pulsar Python SDK

docs.title: Commands and parameters
docs.text: Pulsar Python SDK distinguishes runtime commands from stored or readable parameters.

docs.title: Primary command
docs.text:
A standalone actuator accepts a scalar command:

actuator.set_command(0.5)

The unit depends on the configured mode:

Mode Unit TORQUE N·m VELOCITY rad/s POSITION rad IMPEDANCE position in rad

Commands must be finite and are accepted only in DRIVE_ACTIVE.

docs.title: Mode-specific command fields
docs.text:
from pulsar_sdk import ControlParams

actuator.set_command({
    ControlParams.COMMAND: 0.5,
    ControlParams.VELOCITY_KP: 1.2,
})

Every mapping requires ControlParams.COMMAND. Optional fields may use NaN to keep their current value.

Field Allowed modes D_AXIS_CURRENT_KP, D_AXIS_CURRENT_KI torque Q_AXIS_CURRENT_KP, Q_AXIS_CURRENT_KI torque FEEDFORWARD_GAIN velocity, position, impedance VELOCITY_KP, VELOCITY_KI velocity, position TORQUE_FEEDFORWARD velocity, position, impedance POSITION_KP position IMPEDANCE_STIFFNESS, IMPEDANCE_DAMPING, IMPEDANCE_INERTIA impedance IMPEDANCE_VELOCITY_COMMANDED, IMPEDANCE_ACCELERATION_COMMANDED impedance

docs.title: Group commands
docs.text:
A group or platform batch may select only some members. Omitted actuators keep their previous device command, and every selected actuator mapping must include ControlParams.COMMAND.

arm.set_commands({
    "shoulder": {ControlParams.COMMAND: 0.2},
    "elbow": {ControlParams.COMMAND: -0.2},
})

Direct batch failures raise CommandTransmissionError. Its successful_members field identifies writes completed before the failure.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Read parameters with enum identity preserved:

from pulsar_sdk import Parameters

values = actuator.read_parameters((
    Parameters.TORQUE_LIMIT,
    Parameters.POSITION_KP,
))

Write parameters only while drive output is inactive:

actuator.set_parameters({
    Parameters.TORQUE_LIMIT: 2.0,
    Parameters.POSITION_KP: 0.8,
})

Use dedicated methods for mode, commands, gain presets, address, telemetry rate, and persistence.

docs.title: Unified group or platform updates
docs.text: Parameter and preset methods accept unify=True to apply one value across represented actuators. Commands intentionally do not support unify=True.

docs.title: Atomicity
docs.text:
Validation occurs before transmission, but parameter, preset, and member command writes are not transactional. A transport failure can leave earlier writes applied and later writes unapplied.

Direct batch failures raise CommandTransmissionError; successful_members identifies writes completed before the failure. Callback-path transmission failures instead latch a host error and run the configured safety policy.

See the API reference for every parameter and exact validation rule.

docs.title: Core concepts and workflow
docs.text: Pulsar Python SDK

docs.title: Core concepts and workflow
docs.text:
Pulsar Python SDK uses four layers: an execution domain owns communication or simulation time, an actuator represents one physical or virtual device, a group coordinates actuators that run together, and a platform coordinates groups across a complete robot.

You only need the layers that match the application. A single actuator can be used directly; groups and platforms become useful as the system grows.

docs.title: Object model
docs.text: Concept Responsibility Important boundary ExecutionDomain Owns one transport or simulation clock, its callback worker, telemetry watchdog, and connected actuator leases. One direct USB link, one USB-to-CAN adapter, or one virtual simulation clock. Actuator Represents one physical or virtual actuator and exposes lifecycle, commands, telemetry, parameters, and status. Belongs to exactly one domain and at most one active group. ActuatorGroup Gives stable names to actuators controlled in one mode and one domain. It coordinates lifecycle, complete telemetry batches, callbacks, and group safety. Every member must share the same domain and control mode. Platform Coordinates named groups as one application-level robot. It can connect, configure, enable, disable, and recover them together. May span domains, but does not merge their telemetry or synchronize their clocks.

docs.title: Execution domains are resource boundaries
docs.text:
Choose a domain from the connection being controlled:

Domain Owns PcpOverUsb one direct-USB actuator at address 0 PcpOverCan one USB-to-CAN adapter and the actuator addresses on its bus VirtualWorld one deterministic simulation clock and its virtual actuators

A connected actuator holds a lease on its domain. Calling domain.disconnect() while an actuator still uses it raises ResourceBusyError; disconnect or close the actuator or group first.

Domains are also callback and timing boundaries. One worker handles callbacks for each domain, and each VirtualWorld advances on its own simulation clock.

docs.title: Physical and virtual actuators
docs.text:
PulsarActuatorReal and PulsarActuatorVirtual share the same lifecycle, modes, commands, grouping, callbacks, parameters, and status model.

Physical actuator Virtual actuator Communicates through PcpOverUsb or PcpOverCan. Runs an AUGUR Digital Twin model inside VirtualWorld. State changes complete after the requested state is reported by the device. State and telemetry advance deterministically when the world steps. Uses address 0 on direct USB or a unique CAN address. Uses a unique address within its virtual world. Communication loss means the physical state is unknown. Simulation time and model state remain owned by the application.

Backend-specific operations are reported through Capability and FeatureResult; applications can check support without changing the common workflow.

docs.title: Groups and platforms
docs.text:
Use an ActuatorGroup when actuators share a domain and should be configured, enabled, commanded, and protected together. Member names and mappings are read-only for the life of the group. Closing a group detaches its actuators so they can be placed in another group.

Use a Platform when an application has several groups, including groups on different CAN adapters or a mixture of physical and virtual domains. A platform coordinates lifecycle and propagates active safety, but each group still receives telemetry and runs callbacks independently.

from pulsar_sdk import ActuatorGroup, PcpOverCan, Platform, PulsarActuatorReal

right_can = PcpOverCan("<right-adapter-port>")
left_can = PcpOverCan("<left-adapter-port>")

right_arm = ActuatorGroup(
    "right_arm",
    {
        "shoulder": PulsarActuatorReal(right_can, address=23),
        "elbow": PulsarActuatorReal(right_can, address=24),
    },
)
left_arm = ActuatorGroup(
    "left_arm",
    {
        "shoulder": PulsarActuatorReal(left_can, address=23),
        "elbow": PulsarActuatorReal(left_can, address=24),
    },
)

robot = Platform({"right_arm": right_arm, "left_arm": left_arm})

Replace the port placeholders with values returned by PcpOverCan.list_ports(). The repeated addresses are valid because each CAN adapter is a separate domain.

docs.title: Names, commands, telemetry, and units
docs.text:
SDK types use PascalCase; methods, arguments, and fields use snake_case. A value sent to an actuator is a command, while a value reported by an actuator or model is telemetry.

Physical quantities use SI units unless a name states otherwise, such as _ms for milliseconds or _hz for hertz. The primary command unit depends on the configured control mode.

docs.title: Core workflow
docs.text: Constructors validate names, addresses, and membership, but perform no I/O. Connection and model loading happen when connect() is called or a context manager is entered.

docs.title: Recommended order
docs.text:
1. Construct domains, actuators, groups, and optionally a platform.
  2. Connect or enter the object's context manager.
  3. Configure the control mode and periodic telemetry.
  4. Optionally zero position.
  5. Register telemetry, control, or diagnostic callbacks.
  6. Enable drive output.
  7. Send commands or run the application controller.
  8. Disable before changing mode, changing writable parameters, or shutting down.
  9. Disconnect or exit the context manager.

docs.title: One physical actuator
docs.text:
from pulsar_sdk import ControlConfiguration, Mode, PcpOverUsb, PulsarActuatorReal

actuator = PulsarActuatorReal(PcpOverUsb(), address=0)

with actuator:
    actuator.configure(ControlConfiguration(Mode.VELOCITY))
    actuator.enable()
    actuator.set_command(0.5)  # rad/s
    actuator.disable()

Entering the context manager connects the actuator and acquires its domain. Exiting attempts a safe disconnect and releases the domain lease.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from pulsar_sdk import ControlConfiguration, Mode, TelemetryItems

configuration = ControlConfiguration(
    mode=Mode.POSITION,
    telemetry_items=(
        TelemetryItems.POSITION,
        TelemetryItems.VELOCITY,
        TelemetryItems.TIMESTAMP_MS,
    ),
    telemetry_rate_hz=500,
)

A configuration accepts at most 12 unique telemetry items. The periodic rate is 0 to disable periodic telemetry or 1..10_000 Hz. Configuration does not enable drive output.

docs.title: Commands and units
docs.text:
Mode Primary command Mode.TORQUE torque in N·m Mode.VELOCITY angular velocity in rad/s Mode.POSITION position in rad Mode.IMPEDANCE position in rad, with optional impedance fields

Commands must be finite and are effective only in DRIVE_ACTIVE. See Commands and parameters for command mappings, batches, and stored parameters.

docs.title: Lifecycle ownership
docs.text:
When an actuator belongs to a group, lifecycle operations such as configure(), enable(), disable(), clear_faults(), recover(), and resume() route through the group. This prevents one member from silently changing shared group state.

A platform applies lifecycle operations to its groups in order and attempts safety-critical cleanup across all affected groups before reporting an aggregate failure. These operations are coordinated, not transactional: a transport failure can occur after an earlier actuator or group was updated.

docs.title: Shutdown and unknown state
docs.text:
disable() enters CONFIG_AND_TELEM: drive output is inactive while runtime telemetry remains available. Explicit physical disconnect then attempts to reach and observe INIT_CONFIG before releasing the transport.

Do not rely on Python object destruction for hardware safety. Use disable() and disconnect(), or the context-manager forms of actuators, groups, and platforms.

Warning

If communication is lost, the physical actuator state is unknown. Software cannot confirm that unreachable hardware is safe.

docs.title: Telemetry logging
docs.text:
import csv
from time import sleep

from pulsar_sdk import (
    ControlConfiguration,
    Mode,
    PcpOverUsb,
    PulsarActuatorReal,
    TelemetryItems,
)

items = (TelemetryItems.POSITION, TelemetryItems.VELOCITY)
actuator = PulsarActuatorReal(PcpOverUsb(), address=0)

with actuator, open("telemetry.csv", "w", newline="") as output:
    writer = csv.writer(output)
    writer.writerow(("position_rad", "velocity_rad_s"))

    def log_sample(address, telemetry):
        writer.writerow((telemetry[items[0]], telemetry[items[1]]))

    actuator.configure(ControlConfiguration(Mode.VELOCITY, items, 100))
    actuator.set_telemetry_callback(log_sample)
    actuator.enable()
    actuator.set_command(0.0)
    sleep(2)
    actuator.disable()
    actuator.set_telemetry_callback(None)

docs.title: Multiple actuators in one group
docs.text:
arm.set_commands({
    "shoulder": {ControlParams.COMMAND: 0.2},
    "elbow": {ControlParams.COMMAND: -0.2},

docs.title: Platform callback
docs.text:
def controller(metadata, telemetry):
    return {
        name: {ControlParams.COMMAND: 0.0}
        for name in telemetry
    }

robot.set_control_callback(controller)

The callback runs independently for each group. Use metadata.group_name when behavior differs by group.

docs.title: Diagnostics and recovery
docs.text:
status = arm.status
if status.last_host_error is not None:
    # Fix the reported cause first.
    if arm.clear_faults():
        arm.resume()

If diagnostic safety entered INIT_CONFIG, use recover() after the physical condition is clear.

docs.title: Two CAN domains in one platform
docs.text:
Use a separate PcpOverCan domain for each USB-to-CAN adapter. The platform coordinates lifecycle and safety, while each group keeps its own telemetry stream and callback timing.

from pulsar_sdk import (
    ActuatorGroup,
    ControlConfiguration,
    ControlParams,
    Mode,
    PcpOverCan,
    Platform,
    PulsarActuatorReal,
    TelemetryItems,
)

right_can = PcpOverCan("<right-adapter-port>")
left_can = PcpOverCan("<left-adapter-port>")

right_arm = ActuatorGroup(
    "right_arm",
    {
        "shoulder": PulsarActuatorReal(right_can, address=23),
        "elbow": PulsarActuatorReal(right_can, address=24),
    },
)
left_arm = ActuatorGroup(
    "left_arm",
    {
        "shoulder": PulsarActuatorReal(left_can, address=23),
        "elbow": PulsarActuatorReal(left_can, address=24),
    },
)
robot = Platform({"right_arm": right_arm, "left_arm": left_arm})
configuration = ControlConfiguration(
    mode=Mode.IMPEDANCE,
    telemetry_items=(
        TelemetryItems.POSITION,
        TelemetryItems.VELOCITY,
    ),
    telemetry_rate_hz=500,
)


def controller(metadata, telemetry):
    return {
        name: {ControlParams.COMMAND: values[TelemetryItems.POSITION]}
        for name, values in telemetry.items()
    }


with robot:
    robot.configure({
        "right_arm": configuration,
        "left_arm": configuration,
    })
    robot.zero_position()
    robot.set_control_callback(controller)
    robot.enable()

    # Run the application control loop here.

    robot.disable()

The same actuator addresses may be reused because the adapters are separate domains. Replace the port placeholders with values returned by PcpOverCan.list_ports().

docs.title: Mixed physical and virtual platform
docs.text:
from pulsar_sdk import (
    ActuatorGroup,
    ControlConfiguration,
    ControlParams,
    Mode,
    PcpOverUsb,
    Platform,
    PulsarActuatorReal,
    PulsarActuatorVirtual,
    TelemetryItems,
    VirtualWorld,
)

physical = ActuatorGroup(
    "physical",
    {"joint": PulsarActuatorReal(PcpOverUsb(), address=0)},
)
world = VirtualWorld()
virtual = ActuatorGroup(
    "virtual",
    {"joint": PulsarActuatorVirtual(world, model="PULSE115-60G", address=1)},
)
robot = Platform({"physical": physical, "virtual": virtual})
configuration = ControlConfiguration(
    Mode.VELOCITY,
    (TelemetryItems.VELOCITY,),
    100,
)


def controller(metadata, telemetry):
    return {
        "joint": {ControlParams.COMMAND: 0.0}
    }


with robot:
    robot.configure({"physical": configuration, "virtual": configuration})
    robot.set_control_callback(controller)
    robot.enable()

    # Physical telemetry arrives from its serial domain. The application must
    # explicitly advance the independent virtual simulation domain.
    for _ in range(100):
        world.step()

    robot.disable()

A platform coordinates lifecycle and safety across these groups, but it does not merge their telemetry or synchronize their independent clocks.

Warning

Motion examples must be validated on the intended hardware and mechanism before publication or reuse. Start with conservative commands and limits.

docs.title: Groups and platforms
docs.text: Pulsar Python SDK

docs.title: Groups and platforms
docs.text: Use an ActuatorGroup for named actuators that share one execution domain and one control mode. Use a Platform to coordinate one or more groups, including groups on different domains.

docs.title: Actuator group
docs.text:
from pulsar_sdk import ActuatorGroup, PcpOverCan, PulsarActuatorReal

can = PcpOverCan()
arm = ActuatorGroup(
    "arm",
    {
        "shoulder": PulsarActuatorReal(can, 0x10),
        "elbow": PulsarActuatorReal(can, 0x11),
    },
)

Group rules:

  • every member belongs to the same domain;
  • every member uses the same control mode;
  • an actuator belongs to at most one active group;
  • names and mappings remain stable and read-only;
  • closing a group detaches its members for reuse.

docs.title: Configure and command a group
docs.text:
from pulsar_sdk import ControlConfiguration, ControlParams, Mode

with arm:
    arm.configure(ControlConfiguration(Mode.VELOCITY))
    arm.enable()
    arm.set_commands({
        "shoulder": {ControlParams.COMMAND: 0.2},
        "elbow": {ControlParams.COMMAND: -0.2},
    })
    arm.disable()

A selected command batch may contain only some members; omitted members retain their previous device command. The whole selected batch is validated before writes begin, but member transmission is sequential rather than transactional.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text:
from pulsar_sdk import Platform

robot = Platform({
    "right_arm": right_arm,
    "left_arm": left_arm,
})

A platform:

  • keeps a stable, read-only mapping of group names;
  • coordinates connect, configure, enable, disable, and recovery;
  • can span several execution domains;
  • propagates active safety across its groups;
  • does not merge telemetry batches across domains;
  • does not claim cross-domain clock synchronization.

docs.title: Configure a platform
docs.text:
configuration = ControlConfiguration(Mode.IMPEDANCE)

with robot:
    robot.configure({
        "right_arm": configuration,
        "left_arm": configuration,
    })
    robot.enable()
    robot.disable()

Platform operations validate selected groups before writing and attempt safety-critical cleanup across all groups before reporting aggregate failures. They are not transactional across actuators or domains.

docs.title: Lifecycle routing
docs.text: If an actuator belongs to a group, lifecycle operations invoked through that actuator route through the group. This prevents one member from silently changing the shared group lifecycle.

docs.title: Install Pulsar Python SDK
docs.text: Pixi is the recommended package and environment manager for Pulsar SDK projects. It installs Python and native dependencies together, pins them per project, and provides the same project commands on Linux and Windows.

docs.title: Install Pixi
docs.text:
LinuxWindows PowerShell 
curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm -useb https://pixi.sh/install.ps1 | iex"

Restart the terminal after installation, then create a project and add the public Pulsar channel:

pixi init my-pulsar-project
cd my-pulsar-project
pixi workspace channel add --prepend https://prefix.dev/pulsarhri/pulsar-forge

pixi add pulsar-assets

pixi run python -c "import pulsar_sdk; print('Pulsar Python SDK installed')"
pixi run pulsar-cli --help
